# Umbraco Rules

Project conventions, enforced by code in `Umbraco.Bench.Umbraco` where possible. The short version of the ten UmbraCommandments.

1. **Never put content behind a composition.** Removing a composition permanently deletes its content on every document that used it — no recovery through revisions. Compositions are for meta, settings, CTAs. Litmus test: *if we remove this composition later, is what remains still viable content?*
2. **There are six kinds of document type — file each in its folder.** Page (renders), Block (renders; lives in block list/grid; never used as a composition), Composition (composed onto others; never rendered, never pickable), Data (element; never renders — settings, events, people), Repository (container node; never renders), Repository Item (the pickable records inside a Repository).
3. **Data types never sit at the root of the data type tree.** Built-ins under `/Umbraco/<editor>`, custom ones under `/Custom/<editor>`. `DataTypeSavedHandler` enforces this on every save.
4. **Register in an `IComposer`, not Program.cs.** If `IUmbracoBuilder` can do it, it belongs in `Composers/`. Non-Umbraco concerns (CORS, App Insights) go in `WebApplicationBuilder` extension methods.
5. **Production runs in production mode.** Umbraco Application Url set, `--configuration Release`, HTTPS only, no model generation, no template editing. `appsettings.json` ships configured this way — don't soften it; put dev conveniences in `appsettings.Development.json`.
6. **Aliases are English and camelCase.** No exceptions.
7. **Dictionary keys are PascalCase with dots** (`My.Dictionary.Item`), and a dictionary folder never has values of its own.
8. **Media always lives in a folder.**
9. **The content root only holds Repositories.** The site hangs under the WWW `siteRoot` node; going multi-site means adding another Page beneath it, not re-architecting. Because WWW never renders, the site Page needs a **domain** or nothing answers on `/` — assign `/` for a single site, a hostname each for several.
10. **uSync everything — commit `Umbraco.Bench.Umbraco/uSync/`.** Export is automatic; you should not need to trigger it. On Umbraco Cloud, use Umbraco Deploy instead.

value.markup:
The Model Context Protocol, or MCP, is an open standard for connecting AI assistants to the tools and data they need. Instead of every assistant needing its own bespoke plugin for every system, the system publishes one interface, and any MCP-aware assistant can use it.

That is a simple idea with a big payoff, and it is why we think MCP is awesome.

The Model Context Protocol, or MCP, is an open standard for connecting AI assistants to the tools and data they need. Instead of every assistant needing its own bespoke plugin for every system, the system publishes one interface, and any MCP-aware assistant can use it.

That is a simple idea with a big payoff, and it is why we think MCP is awesome.
Editors rarely want a new admin screen. They want to say what they need and see it done. MCP makes that possible by giving an assistant a well-defined set of actions on the site.

content.text:
The blog is built and running. Both posts and the front page return 200 with every block rendered, and none show "Could not render component".

**What I built**

- **Block element types** (in `Blocks`): Rich Text Block (`richTextBlock`), Image Block (`imageBlock`, with caption), and Callout Block (`calloutBlock`, with heading and text).
- **Blog Block Grid** data type: allows the three block types, each at full width. It is saved at the data type root, which the `DataTypeSavedHandler` should move to Custom. I did not check that move.
- **Document types** (in `Pages`): Blog Front Page (heading and block grid body) and Blog Post (title, publish date, excerpt, listing image, block grid body).
- **Permissions**: Site Root allows Blog Front Page, and Blog Front Page allows Blog Post.
- **Templates**: one per page type, set as the default on each type.
- **Media**: a `Blog` folder with four Unsplash photos: connected-structure, network-lines-dots, code-on-screen and laptop-desk-code.
- **Content**:
  - Front page "Umbraco Bench Blog" under WWW, with a rich text intro and a callout. It has the domain `/`.
  - "Why MCP is awesome: one standard, many tools", with 4 blocks: two rich text, an image, and a callout.
  - "Why MCP is awesome for content teams", with the same 4-block layout and a different image.
  - All three are published.
- **Views**: a rich text, image and callout ViewComponent each, with the matching block-grid adapters. Also a shared `_Layout.cshtml`, and the two page templates now listing the posts on the front page.

**How to view it**

- Front page: https://localhost:44317/ (accept the self-signed certificate warning).
- Posts: https://localhost:44317/why-mcp-is-awesome-one-standard-many-tools/ and https://localhost:44317/why-mcp-is-awesome-for-content-teams/
- Backoffice: https://localhost:44317/umbraco (admin@example.com / 1234567890, from the README).

**Problems and fixes**

- The first run of `/` returned 500. The layout was looked up at `Views/_Layout.cshtml`, but I had first created it under `Views/Shared/`. Moving it was not enough, because the views are precompiled. Rebuilding with Umbraco stopped fixed it.
- The image URLs that first returned 400 were my own mistake: I passed the HTML-escaped `&` to curl. Unescaped, all four return 200.
- No MCP tool call failed.

**Choices I made that you didn't specify**

- The ViewComponent classes are in a new `ViewComponents/` folder, and the plain view models are in `Models/Blocks/`. `AGENTS.md` doesn't name a folder for ViewComponent classes.
- The layout is at `Views/_Layout.cshtml`, not `Views/Shared/`, because Umbraco looks for it there.
- I added two `@using` lines to `Views/_ViewImports.cshtml`, so the generated models and view models resolve in all views.
- The posts' listing images are shown on the front page, and each post has a photo credit caption.

**Not checked**

- I did not check the uSync export, or that the Blog Block Grid data type was moved out of the root.
- I checked the HTML only. I have not looked at the page in a browser, so the styling is unverified.

Umbraco is running in the background (task `bll1ht69k`). I can stop it when you want.
